what_it_does: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a technique that represents a 3D scene as millions of fuzzy blobs (called Gaussians) and renders images by projecting them onto the screen — it produces very realistic images but currently runs at only 2–9 frames per second on a phone, far below the 90 fps needed for smooth VR or AR. The problem, as identified here, is that existing speed-up designs focus on the math side while ignoring how often data has to be fetched from main memory (DRAM — the large, slow storage chip). This paper redesigns the rendering pipeline so that instead of loading all blobs for every screen tile, data streams through in a predictable order: each group of blobs is processed once, and only the screen tiles it actually touches are updated. That streaming order makes memory accesses regular and predictable, which allows the chip to pre-load data ahead of time and cuts down on redundant round-trips to main memory. The approach is a joint redesign of both the algorithm (how the math is ordered) and the hardware (how memory is wired to the compute units), which the authors call algorithm-architecture co-design.
